entities.equation: Cuboid: V = l × w × h  |  Cylinder: V = πr²h  |  Sphere: V = ⁴/₃πr³
examples: Box: 2m × 3m × 4m = 24 m³
Water bottle: 500 mL = 500 cm³
Sphere radius 3cm → volume ≈ 113.1 cm³
common_misconceptions: Volume and capacity are the same (volume is space occupied, capacity is how much a container holds)
Doubling dimensions doubles volume (it multiplies volume by 8)
learning_objectives: Calculate volume of cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, pyramids
Convert between volume units (cm³, m³, L, mL)
Solve problems involving filling/emptying containers
Understand relationship between volume and capacity
key_experiments: Water displacement: find volume of irregular objects

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Acceleration
entities.definition: The rate of change of velocity with respect to time; a vector quantity. Acceleration occurs whenever an object's velocity changes — whether in magnitude, direction, or both.
examples: A car speeding up from rest at a traffic light.
A ball slowing as it rolls uphill (negative acceleration).
key_experiments: Rolling a ball down an inclined plane and measuring its increasing speed.
Motion sensor experiments recording velocity vs. time during acceleration.
common_misconceptions: Velocity and acceleration always point in the same direction (acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity).
Acceleration always means speeding up (slowing down and changing direction are also acceleration).
If velocity is zero, acceleration must be zero (an object can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration, e.g., at the top of a vertical throw).
If speed is constant, acceleration must be zero (changing direction at constant speed is still acceleration).
learning_objectives: Define acceleration as a vector quantity.
Calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
Distinguish between positive, negative, and zero acceleration.
Interpret acceleration from velocity-time graphs.
Explain situations where velocity and acceleration have different directions.

entities.name: Amplitude
entities.definition: The maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position. Amplitude determines the energy carried by the wave — greater amplitude means greater energy.
real_world_applications: Loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude.
Earthquake amplitude sets the shaking damage; radio signal strength is an amplitude measure.
examples: A loud drumbeat produces a wave with large amplitude.
A gentle ripple on water has a small amplitude.
key_experiments: Oscilloscope: a louder sound shows larger wave amplitude at the same frequency.
common_misconceptions: Amplitude is the wavelength (amplitude is height; wavelength is distance between cycles).
Amplitude affects wave speed (wave speed depends on the medium, not amplitude).
learning_objectives: Define amplitude and identify it on a wave diagram.
Relate amplitude to wave energy.
Compare amplitudes of different waves.

entities.name: Atomic Structure
entities.definition: The structure of an atom as a dense, positively charged nucleus (containing protons and neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons in orbitals. The number of protons determines the element.
examples: A carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.
An ion forms when an atom gains or loses electrons.
key_experiments: Rutherford gold-foil model discussion/simulation: most alpha particles pass straight through a thin foil.
common_misconceptions: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed paths like planets (electrons exist in probability clouds/orbitals).
The atom is mostly solid matter (the atom is mostly empty space).
All atoms of an element have the same number of neutrons (isotopes vary in neutron count).
learning_objectives: Describe the atom as a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
Distinguish between protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Define atomic number and mass number.
Explain isotopes.

entities.name: Bohr Model
entities.definition: Early quantum model of the atom with electrons in quantized circular orbits around nucleus, explaining hydrogen spectrum but limited to hydrogen-like atoms.

provenance.source: Bohr 1913

entities.name: Brownian Motion
entities.definition: Random, erratic motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with fast-moving molecules of the fluid. Evidence for molecular-kinetic theory.

provenance.source: Einstein 1905; Perrin 1908

entities.name: Buoyancy
entities.definition: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object immersed in it. This force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object (Archimedes' principle).
examples: A ship floats because its average density is lower than water's.
A rubber duck floats; a stone sinks.
common_misconceptions: Floating objects experience no buoyant force (they do — it equals their weight).
Only light objects float (shape matters — steel ships float).
Buoyancy depends on the object's mass (it depends on the fluid's density and displaced volume).
learning_objectives: Explain buoyancy as an upward force from a fluid.
State Archimedes' principle.
Calculate buoyant force.
Explain why objects float or sink.
key_experiments: Measuring buoyant force on an object in water.
Verifying Archimedes' principle.

entities.name: Change of State
entities.definition: The transition of matter between solid, liquid, and gas phases. During a change of state, temperature remains constant as energy is used to break or form intermolecular bonds.
examples: Ice melts to water at 0 °C; water boils to steam at 100 °C at 1 atm.
Steam condenses on a cold window pane.
key_experiments: Heating ice to water to steam and recording temperature over time.
common_misconceptions: Temperature rises during melting/boiling (it stays constant until the change is complete).
Boiling only happens at 100°C (boiling point depends on pressure).
Steam at 100°C is not dangerous (it contains large amounts of latent heat).
learning_objectives: Describe melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation, and deposition.
Explain why temperature is constant during a change of state.
Calculate energy required for changes of state using Q = mL.
Interpret heating curves.

entities.name: Law of Conservation of Energy
entities.definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one object to another or converted from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
entities.equation: E_initial = E_final ; KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f (conservative systems)
examples: A swinging pendulum never quite returns to its release height — energy is transferred, not lost.
A roller coaster trades height for speed all along the track.
key_experiments: Newton's cradle: the last ball swings out while the first stops — energy and momentum are transferred.
common_misconceptions: Energy can be "used up" (energy is conserved; it only changes form).
Perpetual motion machines are possible (they violate conservation of energy).
Friction creates energy (friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy).
Conservation of energy applies only to mechanical energy (it applies to all forms).
learning_objectives: State the law of conservation of energy.
Apply conservation of energy to solve problems involving energy transfers.
Analyze situations where mechanical energy is conserved vs. not conserved.
Explain why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

entities.name: Coulomb's Law
entities.definition: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
real_world_applications: Static cling and electrostatic painting rely on attraction between charges.
Understanding lightning and electrostatic precipitators that clean industrial smoke.
examples: A charged balloon is pushed away by a like-charged one.
Static cling holds a charged balloon to a wall.
key_experiments: Pith balls: observe repulsion between like charges and stronger force at smaller separations (inverse-square behaviour).
common_misconceptions: Coulomb's law applies to charges of any size (it is exact for point charges).
Force between charges depends on the medium (it does — the constant k changes).
Coulomb's law is the same as Newton's gravitation (both are inverse-square but differ in detail).
learning_objectives: State Coulomb's law.
Calculate electrostatic force between two charges.
Compare electrostatic and gravitational forces.
Explain the inverse-square nature of electrostatic force.

entities.name: Electric Current
entities.definition: The flow of electric charge through a conductor. Current is measured as the rate of flow of charge past a point in a circuit.
examples: A 2 A current flows through an electric iron; phone chargers draw fractions of an amp.
Household wiring carries alternating current.
key_experiments: Series circuit with an ammeter: the current is the same at every point in the loop.
common_misconceptions: Current is "used up" by components (current is the same throughout a series circuit).
Current flows from negative to positive (conventional current flows from positive to negative).
Higher voltage always means more current (depends on resistance too).
learning_objectives: Define current as the rate of flow of charge.
Calculate current from charge and time.
Measure current using an ammeter.
Distinguish between conventional current and electron flow.

entities.name: Density
entities.definition: The mass per unit volume of a substance. Density determines whether objects float or sink in fluids.
examples: Oil floats on water because it is less dense.
A full and an empty box have the same volume but different densities.
common_misconceptions: Heavy objects always sink (it depends on density, not just mass).
Density is the same as weight (density is mass/volume; weight is a force).
All solids are denser than all liquids (ice floats on water — ice is less dense).
learning_objectives: Define density as mass per unit volume.
Calculate density from mass and volume.
Explain floating and sinking in terms of density.
Measure density of regular and irregular objects.
real_world_applications: Ship design (steel ships float because they displace enough water).
Hot air balloons (less dense air rises).
key_experiments: Measuring density of a regular solid and an irregular solid using displacement.

entities.name: Displacement
entities.definition: The change in position of an object, measured as a straight-line vector from the initial position to the final position. Displacement has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity.
examples: A hiker who ends 3 km north of the start after a 7 km walk has displacement 3 km north.
A runner going once around a 400 m track has displacement zero.
key_experiments: Map/playground walk: compare path distance with straight-line displacement using a trundle wheel and a bearing.
common_misconceptions: Displacement is always equal to distance (they differ when the path curves or reverses).
Displacement depends on the path taken (displacement depends only on start and end points).
learning_objectives: Define displacement as a vector quantity.
Calculate displacement from position data.
Distinguish displacement from distance in multi-segment motion.

entities.name: Distance
entities.definition: The total length of the path traveled between two positions, regardless of direction. Distance is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction.
examples: Reading the odometer of a car — total path length travelled.
The length of your round trip to school in kilometres.
key_experiments: Measure a curved path with a string, then compare with a straight ruler line for the same route.
common_misconceptions: Distance and displacement are always the same (they differ whenever the path is not a straight line).
Distance can be negative (distance is always non-negative).
learning_objectives: Define distance as a scalar quantity.
Distinguish between distance and displacement.
Calculate total distance traveled from a path description.

entities.name: Efficiency
entities.definition: The ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, expressed as a percentage. No real machine can be 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated (usually as heat).
examples: A 20%-efficient solar panel turns 80% of incoming light to heat; an LED bulb (≈90%) far beats a filament bulb (≈5%).
Pulley systems reduce effort but lose energy to friction.
key_experiments: Measure electrical energy in and useful mechanical energy out of a small motor or model crane; compute efficiency.
common_misconceptions: Efficiency can exceed 100% (this would violate conservation of energy).
Inefficient machines destroy energy (energy is conserved; it just becomes less useful).
All energy losses can be eliminated (second law of thermodynamics prevents this).
learning_objectives: Define efficiency as the ratio of useful output to total input.
Calculate efficiency in energy conversion processes.
Explain why efficiency is always less than 100%.
Suggest ways to improve efficiency in real systems.

entities.name: Electric Charge
entities.definition: A fundamental property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field. Charge can be positive or negative; like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
examples: A balloon rubbed on hair attracts small paper pieces.
Lightning is a large flow of charge between cloud and ground.
key_experiments: Charging a rod by friction and attracting small pieces of paper.
common_misconceptions: Charge is created by friction (charge is transferred, not created).
A charged object always attracts uncharged objects (a charged object can attract a neutral one through polarization).
Electrons are the only charge carriers (ions can also carry charge).
learning_objectives: Describe electric charge as a fundamental property.
Explain charging by friction, conduction, and induction.
State Coulomb's law and calculate electrostatic force.
Distinguish between conductors and insulators.

entities.name: Electric Motor
entities.definition: An electrical machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy through the interaction between a magnetic field and winding currents producing rotational force (torque).
examples: Fans, washing machines and electric vehicles turn electrical energy into motion with motors.
A toy car's wheels spin because a current-carrying coil experiences a torque.
key_experiments: Build a simple DC motor (coil, magnets, split ring) or observe a force on a current-carrying wire between magnet poles.
common_misconceptions: Motors create energy out of nothing (motors convert electrical energy to mechanical energy with some heat loss).
Motors operate on electrostatic repulsion (motors operate via magnetic forces on current-carrying conductors).
learning_objectives: Explain the motor effect (force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field).
Describe the roles of the armature, commutator, field magnets, and brushes in a DC motor.
Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to predict direction of motor rotation.
real_world_applications: Electric vehicles, trains, and elevator propulsion systems.

provenance.source: IEEE / UNESCO Engineering & Physics Education Framework

entities.name: Electromagnetic Induction
entities.definition: The production of an electromotive force (voltage) across a conductor when it is exposed to a changing magnetic field. This is the principle behind electric generators.
examples: A dynamo generates electricity as a coil rotates in a magnetic field.
Induction cooktops heat pans through induced (eddy) currents.
key_experiments: Galvanometer + magnet-in-coil: relative motion induces current, reversing with direction (Faraday's law).
common_misconceptions: A stationary magnet near a coil produces current (the magnetic field must be changing).
Induced voltage depends on the magnet's strength alone (it depends on the rate of change of flux).
learning_objectives: Explain electromagnetic induction.
Describe Faraday's law of induction.
Explain how generators produce electricity.
Apply Lenz's law to determine the direction of induced current.

entities.name: Electromagnetic Spectrum
entities.definition: The range of all types of electromagnetic radiation, ordered by wavelength or frequency. From longest wavelength to shortest: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
entities.equation: c = f·λ (applies to all EM waves)
examples: X-rays image bones; microwaves heat food; ultraviolet causes sunburn.
Radio waves carry broadcast and phone signals.
key_experiments: Prism dispersion of white light — then discuss how the same family extends beyond visible red and violet.
common_misconceptions: All EM waves are the same (they differ in wavelength, frequency, and energy).
EM waves need a medium (they travel through vacuum).
Visible light is the only useful part of the spectrum (all parts have applications).
learning_objectives: Describe the EM spectrum in order of wavelength/frequency.
State that all EM waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
Identify uses and hazards of different parts of the spectrum.
Relate energy to frequency (higher frequency = higher energy).

entities.name: Electromagnetism
entities.definition: The branch of physics dealing with the relationship between electricity and magnetism. A changing electric field produces a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.
examples: A scrapyard electromagnet lifts cars when current flows.
Electric doorbells and relays use electromagnets.
key_experiments: Oersted's experiment (compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire).
common_misconceptions: Electricity and magnetism are separate phenomena (they are two aspects of the same force).
Only magnets produce magnetic fields (current-carrying wires also produce them).
learning_objectives: Explain that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field.
Describe the magnetic effect of current (Oersted's experiment).
Explain the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Describe applications: electric motor, loudspeaker.

entities.name: Energy
entities.definition: The capacity to do work or produce change. Energy exists in many forms and can be transferred between objects or converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed.
examples: Stored chemical energy in a battery powers a bulb as electrical and light energy.
Kinetic energy of a moving bicycle is turned into heat by the brakes.
key_experiments: Pendulum: height at release swaps into speed at the bottom and back — evidence of energy transfer between forms.
common_misconceptions: Energy is a substance (energy is a property of systems, not a material).
Energy can be "used up" (energy is conserved; it only changes form).
Only moving objects have energy (stored energy — potential — exists without motion).
Heat and temperature are the same as energy (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
learning_objectives: Define energy as the capacity to do work.
Identify different forms of energy (kinetic, potential, thermal, electrical, etc.).
Explain energy transfers and conversions.
Apply the law of conservation of energy.
real_world_applications: Power generation (converting one form of energy to electrical).

entities.name: Energy Loss
entities.definition: The conversion of useful energy into forms that are not available for doing the intended work, typically thermal energy due to friction, air resistance, or other dissipative processes. Energy is conserved overall, but its usefulness decreases.
examples: A bouncing ball never returns to its original drop height.
Heat builds in car brakes and tyres during hard braking.
key_experiments: Bouncing-ball experiment: record successive rebound heights with a ruler and observe the decay.
common_misconceptions: Energy is destroyed when it is "lost" (energy is conserved; it only becomes less useful).
Energy loss violates conservation of energy (it does not — total energy is conserved).
Friction creates energy (friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy).
learning_objectives: Explain what is meant by energy loss in physical systems.
Distinguish between energy conservation and energy dissipation.
Identify sources of energy loss in mechanical systems.
Calculate efficiency of energy conversion.

entities.name: Energy Sources
entities.definition: The origins of energy used by human civilization. Energy sources are classified as renewable (naturally replenished) or non-renewable (finite and depleting).
examples: Coal, oil, gas and uranium are non-renewable; sun, wind and water are renewable.
A solar panel charging a phone converts light to electrical energy.
key_experiments: Hand-crank generator powering a bulb: trace the energy path from input work to light.
common_misconceptions: Energy can be created (energy is only converted from one form to another).
Renewable energy has no environmental impact (all energy sources have some impact).
Fossil fuels are unlimited (they are finite and depleting).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
Describe how common energy sources work.
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of different energy sources.
Explain the importance of energy conservation.
real_world_applications: Power generation (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, solar, wind).

entities.name: Equations of Motion
entities.definition: The set of kinematic equations relating displacement, initial velocity, uniform acceleration, and time for motion in a straight line under constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, and s = ½(u + v)t. They apply only when acceleration is constant.
entities.equation: v = u + at;  s = ut + ½at²;  v² = u² + 2as;  s = ½(u+v)t
examples: A ball dropped from rest falls with v = g·t after t seconds.
Estimating a car's braking distance from its speed and deceleration using v² = u² + 2as.
key_experiments: Braking/accelerating cart on a linear track: measure times and distances to verify v = u + at.
common_misconceptions: Equations of motion apply whenever an object moves (they are valid only for uniform, constant acceleration).
u and v are interchangeable (u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity; swapping them changes the answer).
The equations work for any motion including circular motion (they describe straight-line kinematics only).
learning_objectives: State the four equations of motion for uniform acceleration.
Select the correct equation given the known and unknown quantities.
Solve numerical problems for displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.
real_world_applications: Calculating vehicle stopping distances and reaction distance.
Predicting the time and height of a ball thrown vertically upward.
Analyzing free fall near Earth's surface.

provenance.source: Nepal CDC SEE / CBSE / UK KS4 kinematics objectives

entities.name: Force
entities.definition: An influence that can change the motion of a body — that is, accelerate it. In classical mechanics the net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum. Force is a vector quantity.
examples: Pushing a shopping trolley makes it accelerate.
A magnet pulls a pin toward it — a contact-free force.
key_experiments: Measuring force using a spring balance.
Investigating the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration using a trolley and ticker-timer.
common_misconceptions: A constant net force produces constant speed (it produces constant acceleration).
Force is a property of an object (force acts between objects; it is not possessed by one).
Objects at rest have no forces acting on them (forces can balance to give zero net force).
Heavier objects require more force to move because they have more "inertia" (inertia is resistance to acceleration, not weight).
learning_objectives: Define force as a vector quantity that causes acceleration.
Distinguish between contact and non-contact forces.
Draw free-body diagrams showing forces acting on an object.
Calculate net force from multiple forces acting on an object.
Apply F = m·a to calculate force, mass, or acceleration.

entities.name: Free Fall
entities.definition: Motion under the influence of gravitational force alone, with no other forces (especially air resistance) acting. In free fall, all objects experience the same acceleration regardless of mass, provided air resistance is negligible.
examples: A dropped stone falls under gravity when air resistance is negligible.
A skydiver stops accelerating at terminal velocity.
key_experiments: Dropping objects of different masses in a vacuum chamber.
Measuring g using a falling object and timer.
common_misconceptions: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones (in vacuum, all fall at the same rate).
Free fall means the object is falling downward (moving upward under gravity alone is also free fall).
Gravity is stronger on heavier objects (gravitational acceleration is independent of mass).
learning_objectives: Describe free fall as motion with constant acceleration due to gravity.
Use the equations of motion for free-fall calculations.
Explain why mass does not affect free-fall acceleration in vacuum.
Analyze vertical motion including both upward and downward segments.
real_world_applications: Dropping objects to measure gravitational acceleration.

entities.name: Frequency
entities.definition: The number of complete wave cycles passing a given point per unit time. Frequency determines the pitch of sound and the color of light.
real_world_applications: Radio and TV broadcast on assigned frequencies.
Mains electricity is 50 Hz; the pitch of a musical note is set by its frequency.
examples: Radio stations broadcast at different frequencies; mains electricity is 50 Hz.
A humming insect beats its wings faster than a bee — a higher frequency.
key_experiments: Tuning forks of different pitches viewed on a microphone + oscilloscope: higher pitch means higher frequency.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency means larger waves (higher frequency means shorter wavelength).
Frequency depends on the medium (frequency is determined by the source; wavelength changes with medium).
learning_objectives: Define frequency and its unit (hertz).
Calculate frequency from period and vice versa.
Relate frequency to wave speed and wavelength.

entities.name: Friction
entities.definition: A contact force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of relative motion) between two surfaces in contact. Friction acts parallel to the contact surface and opposite to the direction of motion or attempted motion.
entities.equation: f = μ·N (for sliding friction; μ = coefficient of friction, N = normal force)
examples: A box is harder to start moving than to keep sliding.
Tyres grip the road; without friction a car cannot brake or corner.
key_experiments: Measuring the force needed to start sliding an object (static friction) vs. keep it sliding (kinetic friction).
Investigating how surface type and normal force affect friction.
common_misconceptions: Friction always opposes motion (it opposes relative motion — it can also cause motion, e.g., walking).
Friction depends on contact area (for sliding friction, it depends primarily on normal force and materials).
Friction is always undesirable (without friction, we couldn't walk, drive, or hold objects).
Smooth surfaces have no friction (all surfaces have some friction; even "smooth" surfaces have microscopic irregularities).
learning_objectives: Identify the direction of frictional force in physical situations.
Distinguish between static and kinetic friction.
Explain factors affecting friction.
Analyze forces on objects with friction present.
Solve problems involving friction on horizontal and inclined surfaces.
real_world_applications: Wear on machinery (friction as a source of energy loss).

entities.name: Electric Generator
entities.definition: A machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction, forcing electric charge to flow through an external circuit by rotating a coil in a magnetic field.
examples: Bicycle dynamos light a lamp as the wheel spins the rotor.
Hydroelectric and thermal power stations rotate large generators.
key_experiments: Hand-crank a generator to light an LED; reversing the spin reverses the polarity.
common_misconceptions: Generators create electric charge (generators move existing free charges in conductors via magnetic induction).
Generators produce 100% efficient electrical power (some mechanical energy is dissipated as thermal energy).
learning_objectives: Explain how mechanical rotation induces an alternating electromotive force (AC voltage).
Compare alternating current (AC) generators (slip rings) with direct current (DC) generators (split-ring commutator).
Apply Fleming's right-hand rule to predict direction of induced current.
real_world_applications: Hydroelectric, wind turbine, and thermal power plant generators.
Portable emergency power generators and bicycle dynamos.

provenance.source: IEEE / IUPAP Physics Education Standards

entities.name: Graphical Analysis of Motion
entities.definition: The use of graphs to represent and analyze motion. Distance-time and velocity-time graphs provide visual tools for understanding motion and extracting quantitative information.
examples: Distance-time graphs show a train at rest, moving steadily, and stopping.
The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
key_experiments: Walk in front of a motion sensor to plot live distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
common_misconceptions: The slope of a distance-time graph is acceleration (it is velocity).
The area under a velocity-time graph is distance (it is displacement).
Curved graphs always mean acceleration (depends on the graph type).
learning_objectives: Plot and interpret distance-time graphs.
Plot and interpret velocity-time graphs.
Calculate speed/velocity from the slope of a distance-time graph.
Calculate acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph.
Calculate displacement from the area under a velocity-time graph.

entities.name: Gravitation
entities.definition: The natural phenomenon by which all objects with mass or energy are attracted toward one another. Gravitation is a fundamental interaction that governs the motion of planets, stars, galaxies, and the structure of the universe.
examples: A dropped ball falls to the ground; the Moon is held in orbit by Earth's gravity.
Weight changes slightly between sea level and a mountain top.
key_experiments: Galileo-style inclined plane: uniform acceleration under gravity can be timed and graphed.
common_misconceptions: Gravity only exists on Earth (gravitation is universal — it acts between all masses).
Gravity requires air to act (gravitation acts through vacuum).
Lighter objects experience no gravity (all masses experience gravitational attraction).
learning_objectives: Describe gravitation as a universal attractive force between masses.
Explain why objects fall toward Earth.
Distinguish between gravitation and gravity (gravity is Earth's gravitational pull).
real_world_applications: Tides (Moon's gravitational pull on Earth's oceans).

entities.name: Gravitational Acceleration
entities.definition: The acceleration experienced by an object solely under the influence of Earth's gravity, near the Earth's surface. It is approximately constant for all objects, regardless of their mass.
examples: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface — every freely falling object accelerates at this rate.
In vacuum a feather and a hammer have the same gravitational acceleration.
key_experiments: Measure g with a pendulum (T = 2π√(L/g)) or with free-fall timing gates.
common_misconceptions: g is the same everywhere in the universe (g varies with distance from a massive body).
g is a force (g is an acceleration; the force is weight = m·g).
Heavier objects have larger g (g is independent of the falling object's mass).
learning_objectives: State the approximate value of g near Earth's surface.
Distinguish between gravitational acceleration and gravitational force.
Apply g in free-fall and projectile motion calculations.
real_world_applications: Parachuting (terminal velocity involves balancing g with air resistance).

entities.name: Heat
entities.definition: Energy transferred from one body to another due to a temperature difference. Heat is energy in transit — it is not stored in an object (the stored energy is internal energy).
entities.equation: Q = m·c·ΔT (specific heat) ; Q = m·L (latent heat)
examples: A flame transfers heat into a kettle of water; you warm your hands over a fire.
An iron rod conducts heat from its hot end toward the cool end.
key_experiments: Measuring specific heat capacity of a metal using calorimetry.
Observing heat transfer between hot and cold water.
common_misconceptions: Heat and temperature are the same (heat is energy transfer; temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy).
Heat is stored in an object (heat is energy in transit; internal energy is stored).
Cold is a form of energy (cold is the absence of heat; heat flows from hot to cold).
learning_objectives: Define heat as energy transfer due to temperature difference.
Distinguish between heat and temperature.
Calculate heat transfer using specific heat capacity.
Explain why objects reach thermal equilibrium.
real_world_applications: Climate and weather (heat transfer in atmosphere).

entities.name: Heating Effect of Electric Current
entities.definition: The phenomenon by which electrical energy is converted to thermal energy when current flows through a conductor with resistance. The heat produced depends on the current, resistance, and time.
examples: An electric kettle and toaster heat because current flows through resistance.
A bulb filament glows white-hot from the heating effect of current.
key_experiments: Immerse a resistor in water, pass a current, and measure the temperature rise over time (heating ∝ I²R).
common_misconceptions: All electrical energy becomes heat (some becomes light, mechanical energy, etc.).
Heating effect is always undesirable (it's useful in heaters, fuses, and bulbs).
Thicker wires heat more (thicker wires have less resistance and heat less).
learning_objectives: Explain the heating effect of electric current.
Calculate heat produced using H = I²Rt.
Describe applications: electric heaters, fuses, bulbs.
Explain why wires heat up when current flows.

entities.name: Ideal Gas Model
entities.definition: Simplified model of a gas as point particles with no intermolecular forces, obeying PV = nRT. Valid at moderate pressure and high temperature.

provenance.source: Atkins Physical Chemistry

entities.name: Impulse
entities.definition: The product of the average force acting on an object and the time interval over which it acts. Impulse equals the change in momentum of the object.
entities.unit: newton second (N·s) or kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s)
examples: Pulling your hands back while catching a fast ball lengthens the catch time and softens the force.
Crash padding in a car dashboard lengthens impact time and lowers peak force.
key_experiments: Egg-drop landing on foam versus hard floor: same impulse, longer time, smaller force.
common_misconceptions: Impulse is the same as force (impulse is force × time; it measures total momentum change).
A small force cannot produce significant impulse (over a long enough time, even small forces produce large impulse).
Impulse only occurs in collisions (any force acting over time produces impulse).
learning_objectives: Define impulse as force multiplied by time.
Relate impulse to change in momentum.
Explain how increasing collision time reduces average force.
Interpret force-time graphs to find impulse.
real_world_applications: Catching a ball (pulling hand back increases time, reduces force).
Pole vaulters landing on thick mats.

entities.name: Inertia
entities.definition: The tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of motion — whether at rest or moving with constant velocity. Inertia is not a force; it is a property of matter quantified by mass.
examples: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly.
Yanking a tablecloth leaves the dishes in place — they resist the change in motion.
key_experiments: Tablecloth pull / flick the bottom coin from a stack: the stack stays at rest.
common_misconceptions: Inertia is a force that pushes objects forward (inertia is resistance to change, not a force).
Heavier objects have more inertia because gravity pulls harder on them (inertia is mass, not weight).
Inertia only applies to objects at rest (it applies equally to objects in motion).
learning_objectives: Define inertia as resistance to change in motion.
Relate inertia to mass — greater mass means greater inertia.
Explain everyday phenomena using inertia.
real_world_applications: Shaking a tree branch to dislodge fruit.

entities.name: Kinetic Energy
entities.definition: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion. The kinetic energy of an object depends on its mass and the square of its speed.
examples: A moving truck has far more kinetic energy than a bicycle at the same speed.
Wind turns turbine blades — the air's kinetic energy becomes electricity.
key_experiments: Ramp-and-block: objects released from higher ramps (more KE = ½mv²) push a block farther.
common_misconceptions: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed (it depends on speed squared — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy).
Kinetic energy can be negative (kinetic energy is always non-negative).
Heavier objects always have more kinetic energy (at the same speed, yes; at different speeds, not necessarily).
learning_objectives: Define kinetic energy as energy of motion.
Calculate kinetic energy from mass and speed.
Explain why kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Relate kinetic energy to work done on an object.
real_world_applications: Vehicle braking distance (doubles with the square of speed).
Sports (a faster ball has much more energy).
Wind turbines (kinetic energy of wind converted to electricity).

entities.name: Lens
entities.definition: A transparent optical device that refracts light to converge or diverge rays. Convex (converging) lenses bring light to a focus; concave (diverging) lenses spread light apart.
examples: A magnifying glass focuses sunlight to a burning point.
A camera lens forms a real, inverted image on a screen or sensor.
key_experiments: Finding the focal length of a convex lens.
Drawing ray diagrams for different object positions.
common_misconceptions: All lenses magnify (concave lenses reduce image size).
Lenses work by reflection (they work by refraction).
Thicker lenses always have shorter focal length (depends on curvature and refractive index).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between convex and concave lenses.
Draw ray diagrams for image formation by lenses.
Use the lens formula to calculate image position.
Explain how lenses are used in optical instruments.

entities.name: Light
entities.definition: Electromagnetic radiation that is visible to the human eye. Light behaves both as a wave and as a particle (photon), though at Grade 10 the wave model predominates.
entities.equation: c = f·λ (c = speed of light in vacuum ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s)
examples: Seeing a bulb because light from it reaches your eye; your face in a plane mirror.
Fibre-optic cables carry light by total internal reflection.
key_experiments: Pinhole camera: light travels in straight lines, producing an inverted image.
common_misconceptions: Light needs a medium to travel (light travels through vacuum).
Light travels instantaneously (it has finite speed).
Light is only what we can see (visible light is a small part of the EM spectrum).
learning_objectives: Describe light as a form of electromagnetic radiation.
State the speed of light in vacuum.
Explain that light can travel through vacuum.
Distinguish between luminous and non-luminous objects.

entities.name: Magnetic Field
entities.definition: The region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where magnetic forces can be detected. Magnetic fields are represented by field lines that show the direction and strength of the field.
examples: Iron filings around a bar magnet trace its field lines; a compass aligns with Earth's field.
Speaker and fridge magnets have strong nearby fields.
key_experiments: Scatter iron filings (or use a plotting compass) to map the field lines around a bar magnet.
common_misconceptions: Magnetic field lines are real physical objects (they are a model to represent the field).
Magnetic fields only exist around magnets (current-carrying wires also produce them).
Magnetic field lines cross each other (they never cross).
learning_objectives: Describe the magnetic field as a field of force.
Plot magnetic field lines around bar magnets and current-carrying wires.
Use the right-hand rule to determine field direction.
Explain how magnetic field strength varies with distance.

entities.name: Magnetic Flux
entities.definition: A measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area, calculated as the product of magnetic field strength perpendicular to the surface and the surface area.
examples: Pushing a magnet into a coil links flux and induces current; more turns give more flux linkage.
Transformer cores concentrate the magnetic flux.
key_experiments: Move a magnet in and out of a coil connected to a galvanometer — deflection grows with speed and number of turns.
common_misconceptions: Magnetic flux and magnetic field strength are identical (flux accounts for total area and orientation).
A stationary coil in a constant magnetic field has changing flux (flux only changes when field, area, or angle changes).
learning_objectives: Define magnetic flux and calculate its value for a surface perpendicular to a uniform field.
State the SI unit of magnetic flux (weber).
Relate rate of change of magnetic flux to induced electromotive force.
real_world_applications: Electric power transformers and induction cooktops.
Magnetic field sensors and hall-effect probes.

provenance.source: IUPAP Symbols, Units, Nomenclature in Physics

entities.name: Magnetism
entities.definition: The phenomenon by which materials exert attractive or repulsive forces on other materials. Magnetism is intimately connected to electricity — moving charges produce magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields produce electric currents.
key_experiments: Magnetize a steel pin by stroking and observe north-south attraction and repulsion.
examples: A fridge magnet holds notes; a compass aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
Speaker magnets drive the cone to produce sound.
common_misconceptions: All metals are magnetic (only iron, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys are ferromagnetic).
Magnets attract all metals (only magnetic materials).
Magnetic poles can exist independently (breaking a magnet produces two smaller magnets, each with both poles).
learning_objectives: Describe magnetic materials and their properties.
Identify magnetic poles and their interactions.
Map magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
Distinguish between permanent magnets and electromagnets.

entities.name: Mass
entities.definition: A property of a body that quantifies its resistance to acceleration in Newtonian mechanics; an intrinsic property independent of location.
real_world_applications: Cooking measures ingredients by mass rather than volume.
Mass sets inertia and weight (W = mg), and drives spacecraft fuel budgets in orbit.
examples: A 1 kg bag of rice has the same mass on Earth and the Moon.
A beam balance compares amount of matter, independent of gravity.
key_experiments: Balance an unknown mass against standard masses with a beam balance.
common_misconceptions: Mass and weight are the same thing (weight is a force, W = m·g, and varies with gravity).

entities.name: Measurement
entities.definition: The process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known standard (unit) to obtain a numerical value. Measurement connects physical quantities to mathematics, enabling quantitative description and prediction.
examples: Measuring a table's length with a ruler; a measuring cylinder reads liquid volume.
Timing a 100 m sprint with a stopwatch.
key_experiments: Measuring the same object multiple times and observing variation in results.
common_misconceptions: Measurement gives the exact true value of a quantity (all measurements have some uncertainty).
Only laboratory instruments count as measurement (any comparison against a standard is measurement).
learning_objectives: Explain the need for measurement in physics.
Identify sources of measurement error.
Distinguish between precision and accuracy.

entities.name: Mechanical Advantage
entities.definition: The factor by which a machine multiplies the input force. Mechanical advantage allows a smaller force to produce a larger force, though over a shorter distance.
examples: A lever lets a small person lift a heavy rock; a ramp lets you raise a load with less force.
A block-and-tackle halves the effort needed to lift a load.
key_experiments: Measure effort and load for levers and pulleys; compute mechanical advantage = load/effort.
common_misconceptions: Machines create energy (they only transform force and distance).
Greater mechanical advantage always means easier work (it means less force over more distance).
Mechanical advantage can be greater than 100% efficient (efficiency is always less than 100%).
learning_objectives: Define mechanical advantage.
Calculate mechanical advantage for simple machines.
Explain the force-distance trade-off.
Calculate efficiency of machines.

entities.name: Mirror
entities.definition: A surface that reflects light. Plane mirrors produce virtual images of the same size; curved (concave and convex) mirrors can produce real or virtual images of varying sizes.
examples: A concave shaving mirror magnifies; convex wing mirrors give a wider field of view.
A periscope uses two plane mirrors at 45°.
key_experiments: Curved-mirror ray box: locate the focal point and verify ray diagrams for real and virtual images.
common_misconceptions: All mirrors produce the same type of image (image type depends on mirror shape and object position).
Curved mirrors always magnify (depends on object position).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between plane, concave, and convex mirrors.
Draw ray diagrams for image formation in curved mirrors.
Use the mirror formula to calculate image position.
Explain uses of different types of mirrors.

entities.name: Momentum
entities.definition: The product of a body's mass and velocity; a vector quantity that is conserved in closed systems. Momentum quantifies the "amount of motion" an object possesses.
examples: A heavy truck and a light car at the same speed — the truck has more momentum and is harder to stop.
A water jet from a hose carries small momentum but can wash soil away.
key_experiments: Colliding trolleys on a frictionless track to demonstrate momentum conservation.
common_misconceptions: Momentum and kinetic energy are the same kind of quantity (momentum is a vector measured in kg·m/s; kinetic energy is a scalar measured in joules).
A heavier object always has more momentum (momentum depends on both mass and velocity).
Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions (it is conserved in all isolated systems).
learning_objectives: Define momentum as a vector quantity.
Calculate momentum from mass and velocity.
Explain why momentum is a useful quantity in collisions.
Apply the principle of conservation of momentum.
real_world_applications: Car crashes (crumple zones increase collision time, reducing force).

entities.name: Motion
entities.definition: The change in position of an object with respect to time and a reference point. Motion is the most fundamental phenomenon studied in mechanics.
examples: A bus on a straight road — total distance differs from displacement.
A ceiling fan blade moves at constant speed but changing direction.
key_experiments: Ticker-tape timer: even dot spacing means uniform motion; widening spacing means acceleration.
common_misconceptions: An object at rest is not in motion relative to anything (motion is relative — it depends on the reference frame).
Motion requires a continuous force (Newton's first law: motion continues without net force).
All motion is along straight lines (motion can be curved or circular).
learning_objectives: Define motion as change in position over time.
Distinguish between different types of motion (linear, circular, periodic).
Use reference points to describe motion.
Classify motion as uniform or non-uniform.

entities.name: Newton's First Law of Motion
entities.definition: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues in motion with constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line), unless acted upon by a net external force.
examples: A puck glides a long way on smooth ice before slowing.
A book stays on a table until pushed; a satellite coasts in orbit.
key_experiments: Air track experiments showing nearly frictionless motion at constant velocity.
Rolling a ball on increasingly smooth surfaces.
common_misconceptions: An object in motion naturally comes to rest (friction is the external force stopping it).
No motion means no forces (forces can balance to zero net force).
A constant force is needed to maintain constant velocity (no net force is needed for constant velocity).
learning_objectives: State Newton's first law in words and mathematically.
Explain inertia as the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion.
Analyze situations where balanced forces produce no acceleration.
Recognize that constant velocity implies zero net force.
real_world_applications: Seatbelts (passengers continue forward when a car stops suddenly).
Tablecloth trick (objects at rest tend to stay at rest).
Spacecraft coasting in deep space with engines off.

entities.name: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
entities.definition: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.
examples: The Moon stays in orbit through mutual gravitational attraction with Earth.
Ocean tides are raised mainly by the Moon's gravity.
key_experiments: Compare the weight-force between two masses at different separations with a torsion-balance model or simulation (Cavendish-type).
common_misconceptions: Gravity only exists on Earth (gravitation is universal).
Gravity requires air to act (gravitation acts through vacuum).
Heavier objects fall faster (in vacuum, all fall at the same rate).
learning_objectives: State Newton's law of universal gravitation.
Calculate gravitational force between two masses.
Explain why weight varies with location.
Relate gravitation to weight and free fall.

entities.name: Newton's Second Law
entities.definition: The net force acting on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum; at constant mass this reduces to F = m·a.
entities.equation: F = dp/dt (general); F = m·a at constant mass
real_world_applications: Larger vehicles need bigger engines because more mass needs more force for the same acceleration.
Smartphone accelerometers measure force per unit mass to detect motion.
examples: Doubling the push on a trolley roughly doubles its acceleration.
A loaded cart needs more force than a light one for the same acceleration (a = F/m).
key_experiments: Dynamics cart + force sensor: log force against acceleration; the slope is the mass.
common_misconceptions: F = m·a means the force is a property of the object itself (F is the net external force acting on the object).

entities.name: Newton's Third Law of Motion
entities.definition: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction on object A.
examples: A rocket pushes exhaust gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up.
You push Earth backward when you walk; Earth pushes you forward.
key_experiments: Two spring balances pulling each other show equal readings.
Magnets on carts repelling each other move equal distances (same mass) or inversely proportional distances (different mass).
common_misconceptions: Action and reaction forces cancel each other (they act on different objects, so they cannot cancel).
The stronger object exerts a larger force (forces in an action-reaction pair are always equal).
Action and reaction occur at different times (they are simultaneous).
learning_objectives: State Newton's third law in words and mathematically.
Identify action-reaction force pairs in physical situations.
Explain why action-reaction pairs do not cancel.
Analyze forces on multiple interacting objects.
real_world_applications: Rocket propulsion (exhaust gases push backward; rocket moves forward).
Walking (foot pushes backward on ground; ground pushes forward on foot).
Swimming (water pushed backward; swimmer moves forward).

entities.name: Nuclear Fission
entities.definition: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into smaller nuclei, accompanied by the release of large amounts of energy. Fission is the process used in nuclear power plants.
examples: Nuclear power reactors split uranium-235 to generate electricity.
Fission released in a controlled chain reaction also underlies nuclear weapons.
key_experiments: Chain-reaction model (mousetraps and marbles) and how control rods absorb neutrons to keep the reaction steady.
common_misconceptions: Fission and fusion are the same (fission splits nuclei; fusion combines them).
Nuclear energy is the same as nuclear weapons (peaceful applications exist).
learning_objectives: Explain nuclear fission.
Describe chain reactions.
Explain how nuclear power plants work.
Discuss benefits and risks of nuclear energy.

entities.name: Nuclear Fusion
entities.definition: The combining of light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, accompanied by the release of large amounts of energy. Fusion is the process that powers the Sun and stars.
examples: The Sun and other stars fuse hydrogen into helium and release energy.
Experimental reactors such as ITER aim to harness fusion on Earth.
key_experiments: Compare energy released per kilogram in fission versus fusion using reference data; demonstrate a solar cell output.
common_misconceptions: Fusion is currently used in power plants (fusion power is not yet commercially viable).
Fusion is the same as fission (fusion combines nuclei; fission splits them).
learning_objectives: Explain nuclear fusion.
Compare fusion and fission.
Describe fusion as the Sun's energy source.
Discuss potential of fusion as a clean energy source.

entities.name: Ohm's Law
entities.definition: The current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided the temperature remains constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance.
examples: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles the current.
Adding a series resistor dims a lamp — less current flows.
key_experiments: Measuring V and I for a fixed resistor to verify Ohm's law.
common_misconceptions: Ohm's law applies to all conductors (only ohmic conductors show linear V-I relationship).
Resistance depends on voltage and current (for ohmic conductors, resistance is constant).
Ohm's law is always true (it breaks down at very high currents or for non-ohmic materials).
learning_objectives: State Ohm's law in words and mathematically.
Calculate voltage, current, or resistance using V = IR.
Plot and interpret V-I graphs for ohmic and non-ohmic conductors.
Distinguish between ohmic and non-ohmic conductors.

entities.name: Our Environment
entities.definition: The study of how physical processes interact with the natural environment, including energy flow, pollution, and the physics of climate and ecosystems.
examples: Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases that warm the planet.
Switching to renewable energy reduces pollution from power generation.
key_experiments: School energy audit: measure and rank electricity use and discuss where each unit's energy comes from.
common_misconceptions: Environmental problems are only biological (physics plays a major role in energy, climate, and pollution).
Energy flow in ecosystems is 100% efficient (most energy is lost at each trophic level).
learning_objectives: Describe energy flow through ecosystems.
Explain the greenhouse effect and global warming.
Discuss ozone layer depletion.
Analyze environmental impacts of energy use.

entities.name: Photoelectric Effect
entities.definition: Emission of electrons from a material when light of sufficient frequency shines on it, demonstrating quantum nature of light.

provenance.source: Einstein 1905

entities.name: Physical Quantity
entities.definition: A property of a phenomenon, body, or substance that can be quantified — that is, expressed as a number and a reference (unit). Physical quantities describe the physical world in measurable terms, enabling comparison, calculation, and prediction.
examples: Length, mass, time, temperature and electric current are base physical quantities.
Speed is a derived quantity built from length and time.
key_experiments: Comparing measured values with accepted values to understand accuracy.
common_misconceptions: Physical quantities are the same as the objects or substances they describe.
Every property of an object is a physical quantity (only quantifiable properties are).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between physical and non-physical properties.
Classify quantities as scalar or vector.
Identify the physical quantities relevant to a given phenomenon.

entities.name: Potential Energy
entities.definition: The energy stored in an object due to its position, configuration, or condition. Gravitational potential energy depends on mass, gravitational acceleration, and height above a reference level.
examples: Water stored high in a dam holds gravitational potential energy.
A stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy.
key_experiments: Pendulum/roller model: height at the top of a swing converts to speed at the bottom — potential to kinetic.
common_misconceptions: Potential energy is stored "in" the object alone (it is a property of the object-Earth system).
Potential energy can be negative (it depends on the reference level chosen).
Only height matters for gravitational PE (mass and g also matter equally).
learning_objectives: Define potential energy as stored energy due to position or configuration.
Calculate gravitational potential energy.
Explain the relationship between potential energy and work done against gravity.
Analyze energy conversions between kinetic and potential energy.
real_world_applications: Roller coasters (PE at the top converts to KE at the bottom).
Hydroelectric dams (water at height has PE).
Springs and elastic bands (elastic potential energy).

entities.name: Power
entities.definition: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. Power measures how quickly energy is converted from one form to another.
examples: A 60 W bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second.
A machine that does the same work in less time has more power.
key_experiments: Stair climb: measure your mass, the stair height and the time; compute power = mgh/t and compare walking vs running.
common_misconceptions: Power is the same as energy (energy is the total amount; power is the rate).
More powerful machines always do more work (work depends on power AND time).
Power is stored in batteries (energy is stored; power is the rate of delivery).
learning_objectives: Define power as work done per unit time.
Calculate power from work and time.
Convert between watts and kilowatts.
Interpret power ratings of electrical appliances.
real_world_applications: Electrical appliance ratings (light bulbs, heaters, motors).

entities.name: Pressure
entities.definition: The force applied per unit area on a surface. Pressure explains how forces are distributed over areas.
examples: A drawing pin concentrates force onto a tiny point.
Tyres and balloons hold air at pressure above the atmosphere.
common_misconceptions: Pressure and force are the same (force is total; pressure is force per unit area).
Pressure always acts downward (pressure acts equally in all directions in a fluid).
Larger area means more pressure (larger area means less pressure for the same force).
learning_objectives: Define pressure as force per unit area.
Calculate pressure from force and area.
Explain everyday examples of pressure (knives, shoes, hydraulic systems).
Distinguish between pressure, force, and area.
real_world_applications: Knives and cutting tools (small area = high pressure).
Snowshoes and camel feet (large area = low pressure).
key_experiments: Pressure in fluids increases with depth.

entities.name: Projectile Motion
entities.definition: The motion of an object thrown or launched into the air, moving under the influence of gravity alone (neglecting air resistance). The horizontal and vertical components of motion are independent.
entities.equation: Range = v²·sin(2θ)/g ; Time of flight = 2·v·sin(θ)/g ; Max height = v²·sin²(θ)/(2g)
examples: A football kicked at an angle follows a curved parabolic path.
Water from a tilted hose forms projectile arcs.
key_experiments: Water fountain or ball launcher: photograph the trajectory and see the parabolic curve, with range depending on launch angle.
common_misconceptions: A projectile's horizontal speed decreases over time (it stays constant, neglecting air resistance).
The force of the throw continues to act on the projectile (only gravity acts after launch).
Heavier projectiles fall faster (all fall at the same rate in vacuum).
learning_objectives: Analyze projectile motion as independent horizontal and vertical components.
Calculate range, time of flight, and maximum height.
Explain why 45° gives maximum range.
Solve problems involving projectile motion.

entities.name: Radioactivity
entities.definition: The spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable atomic nucleus. The three main types are alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays.
examples: Carbon-14 dating is used on ancient organic remains; radioactive tracers image organs in medicine.
Smoke detectors contain a small alpha-emitting source.
key_experiments: Detecting radiation using a Geiger-Muller tube.
common_misconceptions: Radioactivity is always man-made (it occurs naturally).
All radiation is harmful (we are exposed to natural background radiation daily).
Radioactive materials glow (they are invisible; only their effects can be detected).
learning_objectives: Describe radioactivity as spontaneous nuclear decay.
Distinguish between alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.
Explain half-life and calculate remaining amounts.
Describe uses and hazards of radiation.

entities.name: Ray Model of Light
entities.definition: A simplified geometric model of light propagation in which light is represented as straight lines (rays) traveling through transparent media and changing direction at boundaries via reflection or refraction.
examples: Predicting where a shadow falls using straight light rays.
Designing a simple periscope from plane mirrors.
key_experiments: Shadow-size and pinhole-image experiments with a bright bulb and a card.
common_misconceptions: Light rays are physical objects (light rays are idealized geometric constructs showing direction of energy travel).
Light only travels straight when observed (light travels straight in homogeneous media regardless of observation).
learning_objectives: Construct ray diagrams showing reflection and refraction.
Apply the ray model to explain shadow formation and pinhole cameras.
Explain the limitations of the ray model (e.g. wave phenomena like diffraction).
real_world_applications: Camera lens design and optical instrument engineering.
Eyeglass and contact lens prescription design.

provenance.source: IUPAP / UNESCO Physics Education Standards

entities.name: Reflection of Light
entities.definition: The bouncing back of light from a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
examples: Your image in a plane mirror; sunlight glinting off a lake.
Retroreflectors on bicycles return light to its source.
key_experiments: Verifying the law of reflection using a plane mirror and ray box.
common_misconceptions: Reflection only happens from mirrors (all surfaces reflect some light).
The angle of incidence is measured from the surface (it is measured from the normal).
Rough surfaces do not reflect (they reflect diffusely).
learning_objectives: State the law of reflection.
Draw ray diagrams for reflection from plane mirrors.
Distinguish between regular and diffuse reflection.
Explain how images are formed in plane mirrors.

entities.name: Refraction of Light
entities.definition: The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in light's speed in different media.
entities.equation: n = c/v (refractive index) ; Snell's law: n₁·sin(θ₁) = n₂·sin(θ₂)
examples: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent.
A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
key_experiments: Bending of light through a glass block.
Apparent depth of a coin in water.
common_misconceptions: Light bends because it changes direction randomly (bending is systematic and governed by Snell's law).
Refraction only happens with glass (it happens at any boundary between different media).
Refraction changes the color of light (dispersion does, not refraction itself).
learning_objectives: Define refraction and explain why light bends.
Use Snell's law to calculate angles of refraction.
Explain apparent depth and other everyday refraction effects.
Describe total internal reflection and its applications.

entities.name: Electrical Resistance
entities.definition: The opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor. Resistance converts electrical energy to thermal energy.
examples: A thin wire resists more than a thick one; metal conducts far better than wood.
Heater elements are deliberately high-resistance so they heat up.
key_experiments: Vary the voltage across a fixed resistor and plot current against voltage — straight line at constant temperature.
common_misconceptions: Resistance is the same as voltage (resistance is opposition; voltage is potential difference).
Thicker wires always have less resistance (all else equal, yes — but length and material also matter).
Resistance is always undesirable (resistance enables heating, lighting, and control).
learning_objectives: Define resistance as opposition to current.
Calculate resistance from voltage and current.
Explain factors affecting resistance (material, length, cross-sectional area, temperature).
Use the resistance formula R = ρL/A.

entities.name: Scalar Quantity
entities.definition: A quantity that has magnitude but no direction. Scalars are fully described by a numerical value and a unit, and follow ordinary arithmetic rules of addition.
examples: Temperature 30 °C, speed 50 km/h and mass 5 kg are scalars — no direction.
Energy and time are scalars.
key_experiments: Sort a list of physical quantities into scalars and vectors.
common_misconceptions: Scalars are less important than vectors (both are essential; many key quantities are scalars).
All numbers in physics are scalars (quantities like velocity have both magnitude and direction).
learning_objectives: Distinguish scalars from vectors.
Identify common scalar quantities in physics.
Perform arithmetic with scalar quantities correctly.

entities.name: Sound
entities.definition: A mechanical wave produced by vibrating objects, transmitted through a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) as a longitudinal wave. Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
examples: An echo returns from a cliff; SONAR measures depth by reflected sound.
A siren sounds higher pitched as it approaches (Doppler effect).
key_experiments: Tuning fork in water (vibrations create waves).
Bell jar experiment (sound needs a medium).
common_misconceptions: Sound can travel through space (sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through vacuum).
Sound travels faster than light (sound is much slower: ~343 m/s vs. 3×10⁸ m/s).
Sound always travels at the same speed (speed varies with medium and temperature).
learning_objectives: Explain that sound is produced by vibrations.
Describe how sound travels through different media.
Explain why sound cannot travel through vacuum.
Relate loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency.

entities.name: Specific Heat Capacity
entities.definition: The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 kelvin (or 1 degree Celsius). Different substances have different specific heat capacities.
examples: Water heats and cools slowly — its high specific heat (~4200 J/kg·°C) moderates coastal climates.
Sand on a beach warms faster than the sea in sunshine.
key_experiments: Calorimetry experiment to measure specific heat of a metal.
common_misconceptions: Specific heat is the same for all substances (it varies significantly — water has very high specific heat).
Higher specific heat means the object is hotter (specific heat is about how much energy is needed to change temperature, not the temperature itself).
Specific heat depends on mass (it is a property of the substance, independent of mass).
learning_objectives: Define specific heat capacity.
Calculate heat transfer using Q = mcΔT.
Explain why water is effective as a coolant.
Compare specific heats of different substances.
real_world_applications: Car radiators (water's high specific heat absorbs engine heat).
Cooking utensils (metals with low specific heat heat quickly).

entities.name: Speed
entities.definition: The rate at which an object covers distance — the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken. Speed is a scalar quantity.
examples: A car speedometer reads 60 km/h.
A marathon runner's average speed over the whole race.
key_experiments: Measuring the speed of a moving object using a stopwatch and ruler.
common_misconceptions: Speed and velocity are always the same (velocity includes direction; speed does not).
Speed is always constant (speed can change continuously).
Average speed is the average of speeds (it is total distance divided by total time).
learning_objectives: Calculate speed from distance and time.
Distinguish between speed and velocity.
Calculate average speed for multi-segment journeys.
Interpret speed from distance-time graphs.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Temperature determines the direction of heat flow — heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
examples: A clinical thermometer reads 37 °C body temperature; a room thermostat is set near 20 °C.
Melting ice stays at 0 °C even while it absorbs heat.
key_experiments: Calibrate a thermometer at the ice point and the steam point.
common_misconceptions: Temperature measures heat (temperature measures average kinetic energy; heat is energy transfer).
Temperature depends on the size of the object (temperature is independent of mass — a small hot object can have higher temperature than a large cold one).
Absolute zero is the temperature at which all motion stops (quantum mechanics prevents complete stop, but it is the theoretical minimum).
learning_objectives: Define temperature as a measure of average kinetic energy.
Convert between Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Explain why heat flows from hot to cold.
Use thermometers to measure temperature accurately.

entities.name: Thermal Energy
entities.definition: The total internal kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a substance, associated with their random motion and interactions. Thermal energy is related to temperature but distinct from it — it depends on mass, temperature, and the nature of the substance.
examples: Rubbing your hands converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.
Thermal energy from the Sun warms Earth's surface.
key_experiments: Compare how fast identical cans of hot water cool when wrapped in different insulators.
common_misconceptions: Thermal energy and temperature are the same (temperature is average kinetic energy per particle; thermal energy includes all particles).
Thermal energy is only in hot objects (all objects have thermal energy).
Thermal energy can be completely converted to work (second law limits conversion).
learning_objectives: Define thermal energy as the internal energy of a substance.
Distinguish between thermal energy, heat, and temperature.
Explain how thermal energy changes during heating and cooling.
Analyze thermal energy transfer in everyday situations.

entities.name: Time
entities.definition: The dimension that orders events from past through present to future, measured as the interval between two events. Time is a scalar quantity and one of the fundamental base quantities in physics.
key_experiments: Time repeated pendulum swings and average to measure the period with small error.
examples: Timing a 100 m sprint with a stopwatch.
The time for one complete pendulum swing is its period.
common_misconceptions: Time is the same as a clock reading (time is the dimension; clocks measure intervals of it).
Time passes at the same rate for all observers (at relativistic speeds, time dilation occurs — though this is beyond Grade 10).
learning_objectives: Define time as a fundamental physical quantity.
Measure time intervals using appropriate instruments.
Use time as the independent variable in motion analysis.

entities.name: Unit of Measurement
entities.definition: A standard reference amount of a physical quantity, defined and adopted by convention, against which measurements of that quantity are compared. Units provide the scale that gives physical meaning to numerical values.
examples: The second (s), metre (m) and kilogram (kg) are SI base units.
SI prefixes: kilo-, centi-, milli- and micro- scale the base units.
key_experiments: Unit-conversion practice: convert between mm, cm, m, km and ms, s for measured lengths and times.
common_misconceptions: Units are part of the object being measured (units are conventions, not properties of objects).
Any number can have any unit (units must match the quantity being measured).
learning_objectives: Explain why standardized units are necessary.
Convert between common units for a given quantity.
Identify the SI base units for fundamental quantities.
real_world_applications: International trade (standardized mass and volume units).
Scientific reproducibility (any lab can replicate using SI units).

entities.name: Vector Quantity
entities.definition: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, and follows specific rules of addition (vector addition). Vectors represent quantities where direction matters as much as size.
examples: Force '10 N north' and wind '40 km/h north-east' are vectors.
Displacement arrows drawn on a map.
key_experiments: Walk 3 m east then 4 m north: a 5 m resultant (3-4-5 triangle) demonstrates vector addition.
common_misconceptions: Any quantity with direction is a vector (must also follow vector addition rules).
Vectors are just arrows on paper (they represent physical quantities with real effects).
learning_objectives: Distinguish vectors from scalars.
Represent vectors graphically.
Add vectors using the triangle or parallelogram method.
real_world_applications: Navigation (wind velocity + aircraft velocity = ground velocity).
Engineering forces (multiple forces on a structure).
Physics of motion (velocity, acceleration, force are all vectors).

entities.name: Velocity
entities.definition: The rate of change of displacement with respect to time. Velocity is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction.
examples: A plane flying 800 km/h due west — speed plus direction.
A car's velocity changes when it turns, even if speed is constant.
key_experiments: Motion sensor experiments plotting position vs. time to extract velocity.
common_misconceptions: Velocity is just speed with a direction (the vector nature has real mathematical consequences).
Higher speed always means higher velocity (if directions differ, they are different velocities).
Velocity must be constant to be defined (instantaneous velocity exists at every point).
learning_objectives: Define velocity as a vector quantity.
Calculate velocity from displacement and time.
Distinguish between average and instantaneous velocity.
Interpret velocity from position-time graphs (slope).

entities.name: Potential Difference (Voltage)
entities.definition: The work done per unit charge to move a charge between two points in an electric circuit. Voltage is the "push" that drives current through a circuit.
examples: A 9 V battery provides 9 V of potential difference across a circuit; household mains is roughly 230 V.
Voltage is the 'push' that drives charge around a circuit.
key_experiments: Measure the terminal voltage of a battery with a voltmeter at no load and under load.
common_misconceptions: Voltage and current are the same (voltage is potential difference; current is flow).
A battery creates current (a battery provides voltage; current depends on resistance).
Voltage is "used up" in a circuit (voltage drops across components, but energy is conserved).
learning_objectives: Define potential difference as work done per unit charge.
Calculate voltage from work and charge.
Measure voltage using a voltmeter.
Explain why voltage drives current.
real_world_applications: Electrical outlets (120V or 230V depending on country).

entities.name: Wave
entities.definition: A disturbance that transfers energy through a medium or through space, without permanently displacing the medium. Waves transfer energy and information from one place to another.
examples: Sound travels through air as a longitudinal wave.
Light and radio travel as transverse electromagnetic waves and need no medium.
key_experiments: Ripple tank experiments demonstrating reflection, refraction, and diffraction of water waves.
common_misconceptions: Waves carry matter (waves carry energy; the medium oscillates but does not travel with the wave).
All waves need a medium (electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum).
Waves always move in straight lines (waves can diffract and refract).
learning_objectives: Define wave as a disturbance that transfers energy.
Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Identify wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed on a wave diagram.
Relate wave speed, frequency, and wavelength using v = f·λ.

entities.name: Wave Speed
entities.definition: The speed at which a wave propagates through a medium. Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium, not on frequency or amplitude.
examples: Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air; light at 3×10⁸ m/s.
Deep-ocean tsunami waves can travel at hundreds of km/h.
key_experiments: Ripple tank: measure frequency and wavelength and verify v = f·λ.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency waves always travel faster (in the same medium, all waves of the same type travel at the same speed).
Wave speed is infinite (all waves have finite speed — light travels at 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum).
learning_objectives: Calculate wave speed from frequency and wavelength.
Explain why wave speed depends on the medium.
Compare wave speeds in different media.
